title: HRISTOV v. BULGARIA
summary: In the case of Hristov v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mr. Ilcho Zoev Hristov, a Bulgarian national of Roma origin, brought a complaint against the Bulgarian state. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face procedural obstacles and risks of arbitrary detention within the criminal justice system. In October 1999, Mr. Hristov was charged with petty theft in Sofia. Due to a miscommunication—his court summons was served to another person—he missed his hearing on 4 September 2001, leading the Sofia District Court to order his remand in custody. After reaching a plea bargain on 23 October 2001, which resulted in a suspended sentence, the court failed to explicitly order his release, and Mr. Hristov remained in detention until 30 October 2001, despite a letter from the court on 25 October instructing his immediate release. Mr. Hristov complained under Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alleging that his detention during this period was unlawful and arbitrary. However, the European Court of Human Rights ultimately struck the case out of its list, as Mr. Hristov and his representatives ceased communication and did not pursue the application further. This case illustrates the procedural barriers Roma individuals may encounter in seeking justice, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and the importance of effective legal remedies for Roma and Travellers in Europe.
